hypotheses.justification: Without `hs`, apply the theorem as stated to `t := toMeasurable volume s`. `t` is measurable (`measurableSet_toMeasurable`), so `t` is also null-measurable. The volume on a finite-dimensional real inner product space is an additive Haar measure, so it is sigma-finite and therefore s-finite. Mathlib's `Measure.restrict_toMeasurable_of_sfinite` (Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Typeclasses/SFinite.lean) then gives `volume.restrict (toMeasurable volume s) = volume.restrict s`. `IntegrableOn F s` unfolds to `Integrable F (volume.restrict s)`, so `hint` turns into `IntegrableOn (fun x ↦ (fderiv ℝ f x).normDet) t`. The current theorem, applied to `hf`, the null-measurability of `t` and this rewritten `hint`, gives that for almost every `y`, `(t ∩ f ⁻¹' {y}).Finite`. Since `s ⊆ t` (`subset_toMeasurable`), we have `s ∩ f ⁻¹' {y} ⊆ t ∩ f ⁻¹' {y}`. `Set.Finite.subset` then gives `(s ∩ f ⁻¹' {y}).Finite` for the same `y`, inside a `filter_upwards`. No degenerate case causes trouble: if `s` is empty, every fiber is empty and hence finite. `hs` appears nowhere else in the statement, so the statement is unchanged; only the proof needs the change above.
